steps.say: Wilson disease hides in any child with unexplained liver trouble or new movement problems. This autosomal recessive copper storage disorder traps copper in liver and brain, striking school age children and teenagers first. Any Coombs negative haemolysis with liver disease should raise the question. Think copper early, because treatment prevents damage but cannot undo it.
steps.tx: The **ATP7B gene mutation** defines a treatable copper trap. **Wilson disease** is autosomal recessive copper storage from **ATP7B** mutations on chromosome **13q14**, crippling biliary copper excretion and **ceruloplasmin** incorporation. Copper then poisons liver, brain, cornea, and red cells, so unexplained liver disease with haemolysis or movement disorder in a child demands copper studies.

steps.say: Look at the eyes before ordering a single blood test. Copper settling in the corneal rim draws the Kayser-Fleischer ring, seen in over ninety five percent of neurological cases but only half of hepatic presentations. Slit lamp examination costs little and points straight at copper. A present ring does not confirm Wilson alone, yet its absence never excludes liver disease.
steps.tx: **Kayser-Fleischer rings** put copper on display in the eye. Copper in the **Descemet membrane** draws a corneal rim present in over **95%** of neurological cases but only **50%** with hepatic presentation. **Slit lamp** examination is mandatory in every suspect, and rings fade with successful chelation, giving the clinic a visible treatment gauge.

vis.caption: Kayser Fleischer ring: copper in the corneal rim around iris and pupil. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: No single test proves Wilson, so the Leipzig score combines them. Rings, neurological signs, low ceruloplasmin, Coombs negative haemolysis, liver copper, urinary copper, and ATP7B mutations each add points, and four or more seals the diagnosis. Score every suspect formally rather than eyeballing results. The tally also guides siblings, who need scoring before symptoms start.
steps.tx: The **Ferenci scoring system** converts scattered clues into a verdict. The Leipzig score counts Kayser-Fleischer rings, neurologic signs, low **ceruloplasmin**, Coombs-negative haemolysis, liver **copper**, urinary copper, and **ATP7B** mutations, with **4** or more establishing diagnosis. Borderline scores trigger repeat testing and family screening, never watchful waiting.

steps.say: Twenty four hour urine copper separates Wilson from every other liver disease. Baseline excretion above one hundred micrograms daily, or above forty in children, points strongly at Wilson. After a penicillamine challenge the output above sixteen hundred micrograms daily confirms it. Collect the full day carefully, since an incomplete jug fakes a reassuring number.
steps.tx: The **24-hour urinary copper cut-offs** carry the most weight in children. Baseline excretion above **100 mcg/day**, or above **40 mcg/day** in children, supports Wilson, and output above **1,600 mcg/day** after **D-penicillamine** challenge confirms it. Incomplete collections under-read dangerously, so nursing must supervise the full jug before anyone interprets.

steps.say: Liver biopsy remains the gold standard when scores and urine disagree. Hepatic copper above two hundred and fifty micrograms per gram of dry weight proves overload beyond any doubt. Histology also stages fibrosis and excludes competing disease. Reserve the needle for uncertain cases, since scoring plus urine usually suffices.
steps.tx: The **liver copper gold standard** settles borderline cases definitively. Hepatic parenchymal copper above **250 mcg/g** dry weight on **biopsy** proves Wilson, while histology stages fibrosis and excludes autoimmune or fatty liver mimics. Dry weight measurement beats qualitative staining, so the sample must reach a laboratory that quantifies copper properly.

steps.say: Chelation pulls copper out through the urine, with vitamin cover against side effects. Penicillamine or trientine at twenty milligrams per kilo daily in divided doses mobilises tissue stores, always with pyridoxine twenty five to fifty milligrams daily to prevent deficiency. Take tablets away from food and watch blood counts closely. Improvement unfolds over months, so impatience must not stop the drug.
steps.tx: **First-line copper chelation** mobilises stores through the urine. **D-penicillamine** or **trientine** at **20 mg/kg/day** in divided doses chelates tissue copper, with **pyridoxine** **25-50 mg/day** preventing B6 deficiency from penicillamine. Doses rise as tolerance allows, blood counts and urine protein are watched for toxicity, and neurological worsening early on needs urgent review.

steps.say: Zinc holds the line once chelation has emptied the stores. Fifty milligrams of elemental zinc two or three times daily traps copper inside gut cells through metallothionein, blocking absorption at the source. Separate zinc from food and from chelators by hours. Children tolerate it well for decades, making it the maintenance backbone.
steps.tx: **Oral zinc maintenance** blocks copper at the gut wall. Elemental **zinc** **50 mg** two or three times daily induces enterocyte **metallothionein**, trapping dietary copper inside shed gut cells. Doses sit far from meals and chelators to keep absorption clean, and long term zinc suits children who cannot tolerate chelators lifelong.

points: Months to years, then step down
left.title: Chelation phase

steps.say: A teenager with sudden jaundice, anaemia, and a failing liver may have Wilson unmasked. Fulminant Wilson pairs Coombs negative haemolysis with deep jaundice yet a low alkaline phosphatase, a ratio of phosphatase to bilirubin below two. No chelator works fast enough here. List for emergency transplant at once, since copper driven haemolysis kills red cells as fast as they transfuse.
steps.tx: **Fulminant Wilson liver failure** is a transplant emergency wearing a haemolysis disguise. It combines Coombs-negative **haemolytic anaemia** with marked hyperbilirubinaemia yet low **alkaline phosphatase**, an ALP to bilirubin ratio below **2.0**. Chelation cannot act in time, so emergency **liver transplantation** listing starts with the first suspicious blood film.
